catalog_quote: 2.2 Stress. The assignment of stress (primary, secondary, clitics, etc.) in Mparntwe Arrernte is not entirely clear, and deserves fuller investigation. One rule that covers a large number of lexemes, is that stress is assigned to the first syllable which is opened by a consonant. (26) ineme /inəmə/ [inə́mɐ] 'is getting'; neme /nəmə/ [nə́mɐ] 'is sitting'. One source of counter-examples to this rule appears to arise when there is an initial /a/ and the second vowel is /ə/. Some words meeting this description may have stress on either the /a/ or the /ə/. The name Arrernte /arəṇṭə/ itself may be realised as either [árəṇḍɐ] or [arə́ṇḍɐ]. Other words may have stress only on the /a/, such as ampwe 'old' [ámbwɐ], or only on the /ə/, such as artwe 'man' [aʼṭwɐ́]. new_statements.quote: Each phonological word bears a primary stress. Some basic rules can be stated in terms of (VC) syllable structure: in words of two or more syllables, the second syllable bears primary stress, as in (8a-d); in words of four or more syllables secondary stresses may occur on alternating syllables after the primary stress, as in (8d). Secondary stresses are more likely in citation forms. A final vowel is not stressed except in Imperative forms of verbs and where it is the only surface vowel of the word, as in (8e). [...] Primary stress may be attracted to word-initial /a/, /i/ or /u/ if the following vowel is [ə].

new_statements.rule_in_words: Under Henderson's VC-syllable analysis (every word underlyingly vowel-initial), primary stress falls on the second syllable of the phonological word, i.e. on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant on the surface: merne /emern/ [mə́ɳə], atherrke [ɐt̪ə́rkə], ampetyele [ɐmbə́ɟələ]. Word-final vowel is unstressed except in imperatives and when it is the word's only surface vowel (re [ɻə́]). For underlying VC(C) words with initial /a i u/ there is dialectal variation between initial and final stress (ampe [ámpə]~[ampə́]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more (VC) syllables, secondary stresses may fall on alternating syllables after the primary (atekertneme [ɐtə́kətɳə̀mə]~[ɐtə́kətɳəmə]); secondaries are optional and more likely in citation forms; author notes it is hard to distinguish word-internal secondary stress from phrase-level prominence of a following word's primary stress. In reduplications and compounds each part is stressed on its own second syllable (first part stronger), independent of the alternating rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Primary stress may be attracted to word-initial /a/, /i/ or /u/ when the following vowel is schwa, more likely when the first-syllable consonant is coronal/apical (Arrernte [ɐrə́ɳɖɐ] or [ɐ́rəɳɖɐ], citing Wilkins 1989: 94-5); stress may also be attracted to initial /a i u/ of clitics and compound elements; imperative verb forms may stress the final vowel; monosyllabic clitics are stressed by the primary/alternating rules as part of the host's phonological word. Author cautions stress 'is not always clear and consistent, particularly.. in casual and/or extended speech' and calls the statements preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Henderson 2002 describes Eastern/Central Arrernte (ECA), the dialect mesh around and east of Alice Springs, which includes Mparntwe (Alice Springs) Arrernte; he notes the description 'cannot be extended to Arandic varieties beyond ECA' and cites Wilkins 1989 (Mparntwe Arrernte) for the initial-vowel stress attraction. Breen & Pensalfini 1999 base their study on Eastern/Central Arrernte varieties (fn.21, the five areas of Henderson & Dobson 1994) and say (fn.5) they believe the analysis also holds for Western Arrernte.

new_statements.quote: Further evidence that all Arrernte words are vowel-initial comes from stress assignment and the prosody sensitivity of verbal plural and reciprocal morphology. In Arrernte, stress is assigned within a word to the first nucleus that is preceded by a consonant. Thus, if the word begins in a consonant, stress falls on the first vowel; if the word begins in a vowel, stress falls on the second nucleus (vowel) in that word. [...] If consonant-initial words, such as those in (2c-d), are indeed underlyingly /e/-initial, then stress in Arrernte falls on the second syllable and is computed at some level where the initial /e/ is present.
new_statements.citation: Breen, Gavan & Rob Pensalfini. 1999. Arrernte: a language with no syllable onsets. Linguistic Inquiry 30(1): 1-25.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant: surface C-initial words stress the first vowel (mpwárem, Nénirem), V-initial words stress the second vowel (ikwén't', atwérem); under the authors' analysis that all words are underlyingly vowel-initial (initial /e/ unrealised), this is uniformly second-syllable stress. The optional utterance-final vowel is normally unstressed but 'may be stressed on occasion, as when it is the only vowel in the utterance' (/mpe/ 'come on' [mbá], p.2).
new_statements.exceptions: Final epenthetic vowel can carry stress when it is the only vowel of the utterance (p.2). The authors reject the onset-sensitive alternative analyses of Davis (1988) and Goedemans (1996) in favour of underlying initial vowels (p.4). Historical note p.9-10: proto-Pama-Nyungan initial stress shifted to the second syllable in pre-Arandic with loss of initial C/CV.
new_statements.identity_note: Henderson 2002 describes Eastern/Central Arrernte (ECA), the dialect mesh around and east of Alice Springs, which includes Mparntwe (Alice Springs) Arrernte; he notes the description 'cannot be extended to Arandic varieties beyond ECA' and cites Wilkins 1989 (Mparntwe Arrernte) for the initial-vowel stress attraction. Breen & Pensalfini 1999 base their study on Eastern/Central Arrernte varieties (fn.21, the five areas of Henderson & Dobson 1994) and say (fn.5) they believe the analysis also holds for Western Arrernte.
